reading.synopsis: Paul Sharp, an economist at a post-nuclear-war reclamation agency, seeks psychiatric help from Dr. Humphrys for a worsening phobia of heights and falling that has begun crippling his ability to do his job. Hypnotic-regression sessions using a memory-retrieval 'lamp' surface increasingly strange scenes that do not match Sharp's actual past: a violent beating and a fall through a hatch, then a Phoenix reclamation-project scene Sharp confirms has not happened yet, then a café confrontation with Giller, a constituent pressuring Sharp for special reclamation funding whom Sharp keeps refusing. Humphrys realizes Sharp is not repressing a past trauma at all but is a weak, latent precognitive unconsciously sensing a real event roughly six months in his own future -- Giller will eventually kill him -- and the government's Special Talents Agency dismisses the case as too weak a latent to be useful, noting that precognized events of this kind 'appear to be fixed' and unchangeable even when the subject is warned. The story closes by revealing that Giller has separately and independently sought out his own psychiatrist about an 'irresistible urge to push people' from heights, confirming the murder is approaching from both directions at once, with neither man able to stop it.

structure.form: short story in three movements: the phobia and its hypnotic investigation, the psychiatrist's discovery that the 'memories' are precognitive rather than repressed, and the closing revelation that the killer is being drawn toward the act just as inexorably
movements: Paul Sharp consults psychiatrist Humphrys about a debilitating, worsening phobia of heights and falling that is destroying his ability to function at his post-war reclamation job.

Hypnotic regression surfaces scenes that do not match Sharp's past -- including one Sharp can confirm has not happened yet -- leading Humphrys to conclude Sharp is a weak latent precognitive sensing his own future death, a case the Special Talents Agency dismisses as too weak to be useful and the coming event as unavoidably 'fixed.'

In a final, separate scene, Giller -- the constituent from Sharp's precognized vision -- is shown independently consulting his own psychiatrist about an uncontrollable compulsion to push people from heights, confirming that both men are converging on the same fixed future from opposite sides.
structure.point_of_view: third person, centered on Sharp and Humphrys for most of the story before a final, separate scene shifts to Giller, widening the story's scope only at the end to confirm that the coming violence is being approached from both directions rather than existing solely in Sharp's own anxious perception.
structure.central_device: A phobia diagnosed backward -- as repressed trauma to be excavated -- that turns out to be a forward-facing precognitive dread of an unavoidable future event, with the story's institutional apparatus (the Special Talents Agency) confirming that such fixed futures cannot be altered even once identified, rendering the entire diagnostic effort powerless to prevent what it discovers.

characters.name: Paul Sharp
characters.role: protagonist, an economist and weak latent precognitive
characters.note: His debilitating phobia is the story's central irony: it is not an irrational fear at all but an entirely accurate, if garbled, perception of his own future death, one his conscious mind can neither correctly interpret nor act on in time to prevent.

characters.name: Dr. Humphrys
characters.note: His shift from treating Sharp's phobia as ordinary repressed trauma to recognizing it as genuine precognition is the story's investigative core, but his diagnosis changes nothing about the outcome -- correctly identifying a fixed future does not grant any power to alter it.

characters.name: Giller
characters.role: a Petaluma-area constituent, Sharp's eventual killer
characters.note: His late, separate reveal -- consulting his own psychiatrist about an 'irresistible urge to push people' from heights -- transforms him from a minor bureaucratic nuisance in Sharp's professional life into a second precognitive vector converging on the same fixed event, exonerating him of ordinary premeditated malice even as it confirms his role.

settings.name: The post-nuclear-war reclamation agency
settings.note: Sharp's job -- allocating reclamation funding and repeatedly refusing Giller's requests -- supplies the mundane bureaucratic friction that will apparently culminate in his death, grounding a precognition story in ordinary institutional tedium rather than melodrama.

settings.name: The Special Talents Agency
settings.note: Its clinical dismissal of Sharp's case as a 'latent' too weak to be worth cultivating, paired with its calm assertion that precognized events of this kind are fixed and unchangeable, supplies the story's bleakest idea: that even a functioning, official apparatus for detecting the future is powerless, or unwilling, to prevent it.

motifs: A phobia or compulsion that is actually accurate perception of the future rather than irrational anxiety about the past
Hypnotic or mechanically-assisted memory retrieval repurposed to excavate precognition rather than repression
An official apparatus for identifying extrasensory ability that treats a weak case as not worth saving, even when a specific, foreseeable death is at stake
Two people converging on the same fixed violent event from independent, mutually unaware directions, neither one able to stop it
reading.significance: The story inverts the conventional psychoanalytic model of therapy -- excavating a repressed past to relieve a present symptom -- into something bleaker: excavating an inevitable future that the excavation itself cannot prevent. Its bureaucratic Special Talents Agency, framed as the appropriate authority for exactly this kind of case, responds not with intervention but with actuarial indifference, its assertion that the future 'appears to be fixed' foreclosing any possibility of rescue before the story even reaches its climax. The closing reveal of Giller's own, independently-diagnosed compulsion completes the story's fatalism: neither victim nor killer possesses free will sufficient to alter what both of them can, in their own partial and confused ways, already sense coming.
reading.closing_note: The story ends without depicting the death itself, leaving Sharp's and Giller's converging fates suspended just short of the fixed event both of them have now been shown, by entirely separate psychiatric investigations, to be powerless to avoid.

distinctive_terms.label: Fall
distinctive_terms.note: Tracks both Sharp's literal phobia of falling and the story's structural anticipation of Giller's eventual, compulsive act.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a precognitive faculty that surfaces a real, fixed future event through the same mechanism ordinarily used to excavate the past, and an official finding that such futures cannot be altered once foreseen
a hypnotic memory-retrieval process that produces vivid, convincing 'memories' which are not memories of the past at all, destabilizing the distinction between remembering and foreseeing
